items.quantified_result: 105 kWh battery giving ~140 mi (227 km); with the hydrogen REx, ~350-354 mi (~570 km) demonstrated on a single charge.
items.relevance_to_S3: Shows the REx concept crossing into type-approved production, though at 7.5 t (Class 6-7 equivalent) rather than 36.3 t — useful as the lower-mass bound of the REx product family.

items.name: Nikola Tre BEV and FCEV (with Iveco/FPT and Bosch)
items.what_it_claims: Class 8 BEV and fuel-cell tractors for NA and Europe.
items.architecture: BEV: battery + e-axle. FCEV: SERIES — fuel cells feed the battery only, battery feeds the e-axle.
items.quantified_result: EU BEV: 738 kWh, ~530 km, 350 kW peak charge, 645 hp FPT e-axle (US versions to 1,140 hp). FCEV: ~70 kg H2 at 700 bar, ~800 km, 20 min refuel, 2x70 kWh usable battery, 2x100 kW fuel cells used SOLELY to replenish the packs.
items.relevance_to_S3: Reference sizing for a Class 8 electric traction path and a clean illustration of the series topology's defining property — the prime mover never touches the wheels — which is precisely what S3 rejects in favour of a mechanical cruise path.

items.name: Tesla Semi
items.what_it_claims: Class 8 BEV tractor with a three-motor rear drive system.
items.architecture: BEV. One highway-optimised motor permanently engaged through a SINGLE-SPEED reduction gear, plus two torque-optimised motors that engage for acceleration and grade holding.
items.quantified_result: Three independent rear-axle motors, up to 800 kW (~1,000 hp) drive power.
items.relevance_to_S3: THE STRONGEST SUPPORTING PRIOR ART FOR S3'S CONTROL PHILOSOPHY, in the electric domain: one machine optimised for and permanently coupled at cruise, other machines brought in only for launch and grade. Tesla bought the ratio spread with EXTRA MACHINES rather than with gears. If S3 wants a single-ratio diesel axle, this is the architectural argument for it — and it implies the e-axle must be sized for the whole launch/grade job, with its mass charged in full.

items.name: Freightliner Business Class M2e Hybrid (Eaton hybrid drive unit)
items.what_it_claims: Production North American hybrid work truck, also offered through commercial rental.
items.architecture: P2 parallel: Eaton hybrid electric drive unit sandwiched between a Cummins ISB and an Eaton Fuller UltraShift AMT. Eaton's HEV places the motor/generator between the automated clutch output and the transmission input.
items.quantified_result: Claimed up to 30% fuel saving (some sources ~40%), and up to 60% in utility/PTO applications.
items.relevance_to_S3: The archetypal North American HD hybrid: the electric machine was inserted into the driveline WITHOUT removing a single gear. Eaton's own product definition places the machine ahead of the transmission precisely to keep using its ratios.

items.name: Siemens eHighway with Scania R450 pantograph hybrid trucks (A5/A1/B462, Germany)
items.what_it_claims: Publicly funded catenary-electrified highway trials; overhead lines power the truck's electric motors at up to 90 km/h, with a hybrid driveline for unelectrified sections.
items.architecture: Externally powered electric overlay on a hybrid truck — the extreme form of 'electric path owns part of the duty, ICE owns the rest'.
items.quantified_result: 22 trucks across three German test tracks; >80% claimed efficiency of the overhead-contact-line path; operation to 90 km/h under wire.
items.relevance_to_S3: Shows the state's willingness to fund even infrastructure-scale overlays, and confirms the pattern once more: the tractor keeps its conventional hybrid driveline and gearbox; only the energy source changes.

items.name: Off-highway diesel-electric haul trucks (Komatsu 930E, Cat 795F, Liebherr T 264)
items.what_it_claims: The oldest and largest population of production gearbox-free diesel-electric road-going-scale vehicles.
items.architecture: SERIES diesel-electric with AC induction WHEEL motors and a fixed planetary final reduction — no mechanical transmission of any kind.
items.quantified_result: Komatsu 930E (first AC-traction haul truck, 1996) at 290 t payload; Cat 795F AC wheel motors at 2,600 V; Liebherr T 264 with a 40:1 planetary final drive for 240 t payload; DC bus nominally 1,800-2,100 V.
items.relevance_to_S3: Establishes the boundary of the gearbox-free precedent: it exists only where the engine is fully decoupled (series) AND the final drive ratio is enormous (40:1) AND cruise speed is low. None of those three conditions holds for a 36.3 t tractor at 85-105 km/h, which is why the architecture has never crossed to the highway.

items.name: Gao, LaClair, Smith & Daw (ORNL), 'Exploring Fuel-Saving Potential of Long-Haul Truck Hybridization', TRR 2502, 2015
items.what_it_claims: Simulated parallel, series and dual-mode hybrid long-haul trucks with a 2010-compliant 15 L diesel over a MEASURED freeway-dominated real-world heavy-truck cycle.
items.architecture: Parallel vs series vs dual-mode, all compared against the same conventional baseline.
items.quantified_result: Parallel and dual-mode: 7-8% fuel-economy improvement. SERIES: NO SIGNIFICANT BENEFIT, attributed to internal energy-conversion inefficiencies. Combining hybridization with reduced aero drag and rolling resistance gives a synergistic >15%.
items.relevance_to_S3: The single most important academic result for WS8's candidate ranking. It is a published, DOE-lab, freeway-cycle verdict that (a) sets the honest line-haul hybrid ceiling at 7-8%, and (b) predicts S1 (pure series) will show no benefit on the WS8 corridor cycle. If S1 comes out ahead in WS8, that result needs an explicit explanation.

items.name: Moghadasi, Yasami, Munshi, McTaggart-Cowan & Shahbakhti, 'Real-world steep drive cycles and gradeability performance analysis of hybrid electric and conventional class 8 regional-haul truck', Energy 320 (2025)
items.what_it_claims: Refines the SAE J2807 gradeability criterion specifically for HYBRIDIZED heavy-duty trucks with DOWNSIZED engines, and benchmarks against grade-distance profiles of 14 steep real highways in the US, Canada, Europe and China.
items.architecture: Pre-transmission parallel (P2) hybrid Class 8 vs conventional.
items.quantified_result: Equivalent fuel consumption of the parallel hybrid with refined component sizing is 3.4% to 8.9% lower than the conventional truck over a representative highway cycle.
items.relevance_to_S3: The most directly applicable paper in existence to WS8: it is about downsized-engine heavy hybrids on steep real grades — S3's exact risk surface — and it exists because gradeability is THE thing that breaks when you downsize the engine. Its 3.4-8.9% envelope brackets WS8's 3% advance gate, meaning S3's verdict will be decided inside the noise band of the published literature. Its refined J2807 criterion is the natural external standard for Task 5's fixed-ratio grade-hold floor test.

items.name: 'Modeling the Hybridization of a Class 8 Line-Haul Truck', SAE 2010-01-1931 (Argonne PSAT)
items.what_it_claims: PSAT simulation of tractor-trailer hybridization; mild hybrid modelled as a starter-alternator parallel, full hybrid as a series-parallel with two electric machines.
items.architecture: Mild parallel (P0) and full series-parallel, Class 8 line-haul.
items.quantified_result: Urban: 20-40% for full hybrid, ~10% for mild hybrid. Highway-type cycles: gains fall to SINGLE DIGITS. Regional/long-haul non-plug-in hybrids: ~5-8% vs diesel-only. On moderate short grades, recuperating downhill braking energy gives up to ~8%.
items.relevance_to_S3: Independently reproduces the 5-8% line-haul ceiling from a different lab and a different tool 10 years earlier. Two independent national-lab studies agreeing on 5-8% is the number WS8 should treat as the prior for any candidate's headline.

items.name: NACFE Confidence Report — 6x2 axle configurations
items.what_it_claims: Independent fleet-and-track assessment of running a Class 8 tractor with only ONE driven axle in the tandem.
items.architecture: 6x2 (single drive axle + tag or liftable pusher) — the adhesion state S3 enters whenever its e-axle is disconnected or faulted.
items.quantified_result: 2.5% average fuel saving across track and fleet tests (range 1.6-4.6%); 2-3% and 300-400 lb weight saving for first-generation tag-axle 6x2s; third-generation liftable-pusher versions ~2% with improved traction. Fleet adoption only rose from 2% (2003) to 4-5% (2016) BECAUSE OF TRACTION CONCERNS, manageable only with load shifting, traction control and locking diffs plus driver training.
items.relevance_to_S3: THE PRIOR ART FOR TASK 5's 'diesel-axle-only adhesion on cruise grades'. Twenty years of fleet experience says a single driven axle at Class 8 weight is a real, adoption-limiting traction problem that needs active load transfer to manage. S3 must show its disconnected-e-axle state does not simply recreate a 6x2 on a wet 6% grade — and it cannot shift load onto the diesel axle the way a 6x2 pusher can, because its second axle carries a motor rather than being liftable. Conversely the 2-2.5% aero/parasitic credit for undriving an axle is a real benefit S3 could legitimately claim while the e-axle is disconnected.

items.name: 23 U.S.C. 127 weight allowances (APU and alternative-fuel/electric)
items.what_it_claims: Federal Interstate gross-weight relief for the mass of specific added equipment.
items.architecture: N/A — regulatory boundary condition on every candidate's payload accounting.
items.quantified_result: APUs: up to 400 lb (many states) and up to 550 lb under 23 U.S.C. 127(a)(12) since the Energy Policy Act of 2005. Natural gas and electric vehicles: up to 2,000 lb above the comparable conventional limit, capped at 82,000 lb GVW.
items.relevance_to_S3: The only lawful offsets against WS8's fuel-energy-per-PAYLOAD-tonne-km metric. Hyliion explicitly used the 400 lb APU allowance to halve its effective 800 lb penalty. S4 (BEV+REx) may be able to claim the 2,000 lb alternative-fuel allowance; S3, as a diesel, almost certainly cannot claim more than the APU line. That asymmetry is worth stating explicitly in the payload table.

contradictions.claim: 'No gearbox anywhere' is achievable on a 36.3 t Class 8 combination — the e-axle can own launch from a single fixed ratio.
contradictions.evidence: Every Class 8 e-axle sold for primary-traction duty carries multiple ratios, chosen by suppliers with no legacy constraint: ZF AxTrax 2 dual (the explicit Class 8 variant) integrates a THREE-SPEED transmission to reach 54,800 Nm; ZF AxTrax 2 single is also three-speed at 25,980 Nm; Allison eGen Power 100D/130D integrate a TWO-SPEED gearbox with Allison stating the reason verbatim — 'enabling the high torque required to get heavy loads moving, while also offering the benefit of superior efficiency at cruise speed' (130D: 47,000 Nm at the wheels); Cummins-Meritor 17Xe (44 t GCW) offers up to THREE speeds; Dana's Zero-8 Class 7/8 family is described as multi-speed across 4x2/6x2/6x4. By contrast the only SINGLE-speed Class 8 e-axles in the record are pure overlays that never have to launch the vehicle alone: Range Energy's e-trailer axle at 14,000 Nm and Revoy's 400 kW dolly axle. Independent trade analysis states the rule plainly: for heavy vehicles that must both start on grade and hold highway speed, 'a single-speed setup would require an enormous motor', early direct-drive adopters 'require excessively large and heavy motors that still cannot perform to the same level as diesel trucks', and multi-speed delivers 10-15% better drivetrain efficiency — with a worked example of a 1,200 kW single-speed motor replaced by an 800 kW motor plus multi-speed with BETTER gradeability.

contradictions.claim: A Class 8 tractor can meet its launch/startability duty without transmission torque multiplication.
contradictions.evidence: Industry startability practice sizes the launch path at a TOTAL ratio around 46:1 — a worked Class 8 example uses 800 lb-ft engine torque x 3.73 axle x 12.45 first gear to reach a startability factor of 20.6 (i.e. ~20% grade) at 80,000 lb, described as merely 'adequate for general linehaul' and NOT advisable for more demanding environments. S3's fixed cruise ratio is roughly two orders of magnitude smaller: Daimler's SuperTruck II ran a 1.75:1 axle at 950 rpm cruise, so a cruise-ratio-only diesel path has ~1/26 of the launch torque multiplication of that 12-speed first gear. All of that launch duty therefore lands on the e-axle. At 36.3 t on a 20% grade the wheel torque required is roughly 36,300 x 9.81 x 0.20 x 0.50 m = ~35,600 Nm plus rolling — above the 14,000 Nm that the best-documented single-speed Class 8 overlay e-axle (Range RA-01) produces, and reachable only by the two-/three-speed products (Allison 130D 47,000 Nm, ZF AxTrax 2 dual 54,800 Nm). S3's e-axle must therefore either carry ratios (violating 'no gearbox anywhere') or be sized to a mass that must be charged against payload.

contradictions.claim: Deleting the ICE transmission on a Class 8 truck is a solved, demonstrated move.
contradictions.evidence: It has been demonstrated four times, and in EVERY case gearing came straight back on the electric side. (1) Hyliion Hypertruck ERX — the generator was mounted on the rear of the Cummins engine LITERALLY WHERE THE TRANSMISSION HAD BEEN, and the truck then ran two Meritor 14Xe drive axles EACH WITH A TWO-SPEED GEARBOX. (2) ePower Engine Systems, whose stated thesis was 'eliminating the need for complex heavy truck transmissions' by running the engine at constant rpm, fitted an off-the-shelf FIVE-SPEED AUTOMATIC to a 150 hp traction motor to move 80,000 lb. (3) Wrightspeed's Route 1000 traction unit is 'a two-speed gearbox with integrated motor'. (4) Off-highway series diesel-electric haul trucks get away with no gearbox only via a 40:1 planetary final drive (Liebherr T 264) at low road speeds. Nobody who removed the ICE gearbox managed to end up with no gearbox.

contradictions.claim: Through-the-road / P4 e-axle placement is a good architecture for a heavy line-haul hybrid.
contradictions.evidence: The peer-reviewed comparison goes the other way: the pre-transmission parallel (P2) hybrid is identified as the predominant non-plug-in configuration for Class 8 trucks, 'offering superior fuel conversion efficiency compared to series hybrid and other types of parallel hybrid architectures (P0, P1, P3, and P4)'. The stated structural reason is generic and applies directly to S3: in P3 and P4 'a larger and more expensive electric machine is necessary to achieve pure electric drive, since there is no torque amplification by the transmission', and 'the P4 system cannot benefit from the variable transmission gear ratio'. Every OEM that shipped a heavy hybrid chose P2 and hosted it inside the gearbox — Scania's GE281 merges two machines into the Opticruise itself; Eaton's HD hybrid sits between the automated clutch output and the transmission input; Volvo's I-SAM works through I-Shift; Great Wall built a bespoke 8-SPEED DHT for a heavy truck (P2+P2.5).

contradictions.claim: A single fixed ratio can serve the diesel across the line-haul speed range (S3's 'cruise-plus-margin' engine).
contradictions.evidence: With one ratio, engine speed is rigidly proportional to road speed. Taking the most aggressive real cruise ratio ever fielded — Daimler SuperTruck II's 1.75:1 axle at 950 rpm at highway cruise — the diesel would be at roughly 430 rpm at 45 km/h and roughly 290 rpm at 30 km/h, i.e. well below idle and unable to produce torque at all. On WS8's mandated 6% mountain segment at 36.3 t with a DOWNSIZED engine, road speed collapses into exactly that band, so the fixed-ratio diesel axle contributes nothing precisely where the tractive demand peaks and the e-axle must carry the entire climb out of the buffer. This is the failure mode the 2025 Energy paper was written to characterise: it had to refine the SAE J2807 gradeability criterion specifically for 'hybridized HD trucks with downsized internal combustion engines' benchmarked against 14 real steep highways. No commercial product has ever accepted this coupling: the 'direct drive' modes advertised on Chinese hybrid heavy trucks (Foton Auman's 'efficient direct drive', Great Wall's direct-drive mode) are modes SELECTED WITHIN a multi-speed DHT, not a substitute for one.

contradictions.claim: There is meaningful headroom above S0 for an overlay/split hybrid on a line-haul corridor.
contradictions.evidence: Four independent sources converge on 5-8% as the honest line-haul hybrid ceiling, before any mass charge. ORNL (TRR 2502, measured freeway-dominated cycle, 15 L diesel): parallel and dual-mode 7-8%, series NO SIGNIFICANT BENEFIT. Argonne PSAT (SAE 2010-01-1931): urban 20-40% full-hybrid, but highway cycles fall to single digits; regional/long-haul non-plug-in ~5-8%; up to ~8% from recuperating moderate short grades. Energy 320 (2025), P2 with refined sizing on steep real highways: 3.4-8.9%. Volvo's own long-haul Concept Truck, with I-See topography look-ahead: the HYBRID PATH ALONE gives 5-10% by shutting the engine off up to 30% of driving time (the famous 30% is the whole vehicle including aero). Foton's production data resolves it by terrain: 26% mountainous, 16% highway, 10% overall. WS8's >=3% advance gate therefore sits INSIDE the scatter of the published literature, and S3 must clear it while carrying an e-axle, a pack, a clutch and a rev-matching system against payload.

contradictions.claim: S3's disconnected-e-axle state (diesel axle only) is adhesion-neutral.
contradictions.evidence: Twenty years of NACFE fleet and track evidence on 6x2 tractors — the same single-driven-axle condition — records real traction limitation as the adoption blocker: uptake crept only from 2% (2003) to 4-5% (2016), and traction is manageable only with load shifting from the dead axle to the live axle, plus traction control, locking differentials and driver training. S3 is worse placed than a 6x2 in one specific respect: a 6x2's unpowered axle can be a LIFTABLE pusher whose load can be actively transferred onto the drive axle, whereas S3's second tandem axle carries an e-machine and cannot be lifted, so the classic mitigation is unavailable. Note the offsetting credit: the 6x2 data also shows 2-2.5% fuel saving (1.6-4.6% range) and 300-400 lb weight saving from undriving one axle, which S3 may legitimately claim while disconnected.

contradictions.claim: Pure series (S1) is competitive on a line-haul corridor.
contradictions.evidence: Directly contradicted by the ORNL freeway-cycle study: 'there was no significant fuel economy benefit for the series hybrid truck because of internal inefficiencies in energy exchange', while parallel and dual-mode reached 7-8% on the same cycle. Corroborated commercially: the only Class 8 series product to reach production intent (Hyliion Hypertruck ERX) was cancelled in Nov-2023 for complexity and cost; Walmart's WAVE series-turbine Class 8 (2014) never productionised; ePower and Wrightspeed did not scale. Current series entrants (ReVolt ~40%, Edison up to 50%) earn their headline numbers from PLUG-IN grid substitution and from favourable regen-rich duty (logging, stop-go), not from freeway thermodynamics.

contradictions.claim: Overlay products' headline fuel savings are evidence for what a non-plug-in split hybrid can achieve.
contradictions.evidence: They are not — the big numbers are energy substitution. Revoy claims up to 90-95% diesel reduction (MVTS measured 90.4% on flat terrain) from a 525-575 kWh PLUG-IN pack; Range Energy's certified 36.3% comes from a 200 kWh plug-in pack; Trailer Dynamics claims 40% from an LFP-pack e-trailer; Scania/DHL's EREV saved 90% CO2 by running >90% of km on grid electricity with the generator active on only 8.1% of km. The correctly-scoped charge-sustaining numbers from the same industry are an order of magnitude smaller: Hyliion's tandem-split overlay claimed 15%, best case, in rolling hilly terrain. Any S3 comparison to overlay marketing numbers is a category error.

contradictions.claim: S3's mass penalty is modest because the AMT is deleted.
contradictions.evidence: No commercial data point supports a net mass CREDIT for this class of change, and the counter-evidence is large. Hyliion's much simpler overlay (motorized axle + small pack + controller, AMT untouched) cost +800 lb / 363 kg. Revoy's dolly is ~10 t / 22,000 lb. MAHLE's tier-1 figure for the opposite trade — swapping one third of a BEV pack for a 110-130 kW genset — is ~600 kg. Against that, an Endurant-class HD AMT is a low-hundreds-of-kg item, and deleting it forces mass back in elsewhere: a launch-capable e-axle at 36.3 t (17Xe-class, 420-450 kW, vs a 150-250 kW Class 6-7 unit), a bigger buffer to carry whole grade climbs the below-idle diesel cannot assist, a rev-matched clutch and its actuation, and the park/hold and reverse functions the gearbox used to provide (Dana had to add an electronically controlled parking pawl specifically 'for vehicles without a traditional transmission'). Nothing in the record shows the ledger closing positive.

open_ground: UNOCCUPIED, AND CLEANLY SO: no on-highway Class 7/8 vehicle in the commercial or funded-program record has ever coupled a combustion engine to a drive axle through a single fixed ratio. Across ~35 products and programs the only gearbox-free heavy vehicles are SERIES (engine decoupled) — and even they reinstated 2-, 3- or 5-speed gearing on the traction side, or used 40:1 final drives at off-highway speeds. S3's topology is genuinely novel; the risk is physics, not precedent.

UNOCCUPIED: the specific S3 combination — diesel mechanically driving one tandem axle at a fixed ratio while a DISCONNECTABLE e-axle on the other tandem axle owns launch and low speed. The tandem-split geometry exists exactly once (Hyliion 6X4HE) but there the e-axle was a pure overlay and the diesel kept its full AMT. Nobody has built the version where the electric side is load-bearing for launch.

UNOCCUPIED: nobody has ever claimed the AMT-deletion credit S3 is banking. Every overlay product in the market (Hyliion, Revoy, Range, Trailer Dynamics) advertises 'no modification to the tractor' as a FEATURE and therefore books zero mass, cost or efficiency credit from the gearbox. WS8 will be the first place that credit is quantified — which means it must be derived from first principles and cannot be cited to anyone.

PARTIALLY OCCUPIED — check hard before claiming novelty: the CONTROL LAW 'electric owns launch and low speed, ICE takes over above a speed/load threshold' was demonstrated on a DOE-funded Class 8 by Navistar/Bosch in SuperTruck II (150 kW motor, 30 kWh, S13 engine, 16 mpg, 170% freight efficiency). S3's novelty is therefore narrowly the DELETION OF THE RATIOS, not the blending strategy. Tesla Semi occupies the analogous electric-domain idea (one permanently-engaged single-speed cruise motor plus torque motors for launch and grade), which is the best supporting argument S3 has.

OPEN MEASUREMENT GROUND: nobody publishes spin-drag for a disconnected Class 8 e-axle. S2 and S3 both hinge on 'disconnect makes the drag zero', and the entire supplier literature is silent — no churning, bearing, seal or residual-magnet drag numbers for a 400+ kW axle at 105 km/h. This is a first-principles derivation WS8 must own, and an obvious adjudicator target.

OPEN GROUND: rev-matched clutch engagement of a fixed-ratio diesel axle at 85-105 km/h on a Class 8 — engagement transient, driveline torsionals, clutch thermal duty, NVH, and the failure mode of a mis-matched engagement into a 36.3 t driveline. Zero product literature. Contrast Beijing Heavy Duty's i-Zhuimeng hybrid, whose selling point was 'no clutch disengagement during gear shifting to reduce wear', i.e. the industry is moving to reduce clutch events, not to add a high-speed one.

OPEN GROUND: grade-hold, creep and low-speed manoeuvring with a below-idle diesel. Every product either keeps a first gear or has an electric path sized for the whole vehicle. S3 has neither at low speed if the pack is depleted after a long climb. Task 5's 'fixed-ratio grade-hold floor' has no prior art to lean on and must be derived.

OPEN GROUND: e-axle-fault limp capability. Every overlay in the market limps home on the untouched diesel + AMT — that is precisely why they are overlays. S3 inverts the dependency: an e-axle fault leaves a vehicle that physically cannot start from rest. There is no product precedent for this failure mode at Class 8, and it is a homologation question, not just an efficiency one.

OPEN GROUND: reverse and park. Deleting the gearbox deletes reverse (must come entirely from the e-axle, dragging the fixed-ratio diesel axle backwards through its clutch) and deletes park lock — Dana explicitly added an electronically controlled parking pawl to its e-axles 'for vehicles without a traditional transmission'. Neither function appears anywhere in the S3 description.

OPEN GROUND: fuel energy per PAYLOAD tonne-km is not reported by ANY product in this survey. Revoy's ~10 t dolly, Range's e-trailer, Trailer Dynamics' e-trailer and Hyliion's +800 lb are never charged against payload in their claims. WS8's metric of record is therefore genuinely differentiating — and the only lawful offsets are the 23 U.S.C. 127 allowances (400-550 lb APU; 2,000 lb for NGV/electric up to 82,000 lb GVW), which S4 can likely claim and S3, as a diesel, likely cannot. That asymmetry deserves an explicit line in the candidate table.

CALIBRATION GROUND for Task 2: usable external anchors found — Great Wall Hi4-G at 29.7 L/100 km against a 35.8 L/100 km China stage-4 baseline (49 t GCW, so not directly transferable); Daimler SuperTruck II's 1.75:1 axle at 950 rpm cruise as the extreme downspeeding point; Kenworth SuperTruck 2's 55.7% peak BTE vs ~47% for a modern production diesel (a research peak, NOT a fleet value); and the warning that SuperTruck mpg headlines are often quoted at 65,000 lb GCVWR (Volvo ST2) rather than 80,000 lb / 36.3 t.

SIZING GROUND for S4: the two most current REx heavy-truck data points both sit BELOW WS8's 150-200 kW sustainer band — Scania/DHL EREV used a 120 kW generator with a 416 kWh pack to reach 800 km at 40 t (range extender active on only 8.1% of km over 22,000 km of revenue service), and MAHLE's integrated module delivers 110-130 kW while returning ~600 kg of payload by displacing a third of the pack. If S4's genset can be sized at ~120 kW rather than 150-200 kW, that is direct payload back in a metric where payload is the denominator.

lens: Academic and technical literature (SAE / IEEE / ScienceDirect / MDPI / NREL / Argonne / ORNL / EPA-NHTSA Phase 2 / ICCT / theses). METHOD CAVEAT, load-bearing for WS8: WebFetch was blocked by this environment's egress proxy for essentially every scholarly and regulatory host (osti.gov, theicct.org, sciencedirect.com, mdpi.com, epa.gov, nhtsa.gov, ecfr.gov, saemobilus.sae.org, docs.nrel.gov, semanticscholar.org, arxiv.org, nationalacademies.org, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, wikipedia). Only github.com/raw.githubusercontent.com resolved. Every literature number below therefore comes from WebSearch result extracts that quote the source, NOT from full-text reads, and the WebSearch budget (200 calls) is now exhausted. Treat each as PROVISIONAL-CITED per E13 precedent: usable to bracket a calibration corridor, but any number that ends up load-bearing in REPORT_WS8's headline must be re-verified against full text before ratification. Numbers I derived myself are labeled DERIVED and are reproducible from the stated road-load equation; they are not literature and carry no citation.

items.name: Comparative Study of Hybrid Powertrains on Fuel Saving, Emissions, and Component Energy Loss in HD Trucks (SAE 2014-01-2326; Gao, Finney, Daw, LaClair; ORNL; SAE Int. J. Commercial Vehicles 2014)
items.what_it_claims: Simulates parallel, series and dual-mode hybrid Class 8 trucks against a conventional baseline over city and highway duty, with a component-level energy-loss audit. Concludes series hybrid is 'absolutely negative' for long-haul fuel economy because of the dual-step mechanical-electrical-mechanical conversion; parallel hybrid combined with 50% auxiliary load reduction gives 5-7% in long-haul.
items.architecture: series vs parallel vs dual-mode (power-split), Class 8
items.quantified_result: Motor+generator energy loss: 7.4% (series) vs 1.0% (parallel) vs 0.8% (dual-mode). Parallel + 50% aux load reduction: 5-7% fuel economy improvement on long-haul. Series: negative on long-haul.
items.relevance_to_S3: This is the single most decisive external number for WS8's whole candidate set. The 7.4% vs 1.0% conversion-loss split is a direct, independently published measure of the tax WS8's S1 (pure series) must pay and quantifies the penalty S3 incurs in every operating window where its fixed-ratio diesel axle is out of band and tractive power must route through the e-axle. It also gives WS8 an external cross-check on the Vehicle Zero G1 finding (-2.5% for a locked mechanical path vs pure series) by showing the sign runs the other way at Class 8 line-haul scale, because at 36.3 t and 85-105 km/h the mechanical path is dominant in a way it never was at V2 scale.

items.name: Exploring Fuel-Saving Potential of Long-Haul Truck Hybridization (Gao, LaClair, Smith, Daw; ORNL; Transportation Research Record 2502, pp. 99-107, 2015; DOI 10.3141/2502-12)
items.what_it_claims: Compares simulated fuel economy of parallel, series and dual-mode hybrid long-haul trucks plus a conventional baseline, powered by a commercial 2010-compliant 15 L diesel over a freeway-dominated heavy-duty cycle; then stacks reduced aerodynamic drag and rolling resistance on top of hybridization.
items.architecture: series vs parallel vs dual-mode, Class 8 long-haul, 15 L diesel
items.quantified_result: Parallel and dual-mode: 7-8% fuel economy improvement. Series: no significant benefit (internal energy-exchange inefficiency). Hybridization + reduced CdA + reduced Crr combined: >15% (synergistic, greater than the sum).
items.relevance_to_S3: Sets the realistic ceiling for WS8's ADVANCE bar. WS8's pre-committed gate is >=3% vs S0 on fuel per payload tonne-km; the published state of the art for a well-executed parallel Class 8 line-haul hybrid is 7-8% on fuel alone, BEFORE any payload charge for hybrid mass. Since WS8's metric of record divides by payload and every powertrain kilogram displaces payload, S2/S3/S4 must clear 3% net of a mass penalty that this literature never charges. The >15% synergy figure also warns that any WS8 result claiming large gains should be checked for whether it is silently importing an aero/Crr improvement that S0 does not have.

items.name: Modeling the Hybridization of a Class 8 Line-Haul Truck (SAE 2010-01-1931; Karbowski, Delorme, Rousseau; Argonne National Laboratory, PSAT)
items.what_it_claims: Argonne PSAT (Autonomie predecessor) study of tractor-trailer hybridization. Mild hybrid = parallel with the electric machine in starter-alternator position (P0/P1), enabling stop-start, mild torque assist and limited regeneration. Full hybrid = series-parallel with two electric machines, able to run electric-only at low speed / low power. Finds benefit is concentrated on hilly terrain and is strongly sensitive to drive cycle, comparing a short standard highway cycle against a longer cruising scenario.
items.architecture: P0/P1 mild parallel; series-parallel full hybrid; Class 8 line-haul
items.quantified_result: NONE FOUND at the percentage level in accessible extracts — the qualitative findings (benefit on hilly terrain; strong cycle sensitivity; electric-only at low speed/low power) are confirmed but the fuel-economy percentages were not retrievable without full text.
items.relevance_to_S3: Directly relevant to WS8 TASK 1's cycle design: this paper's central finding is that Class 8 hybrid benefit is a function of terrain, not of architecture alone, and that a short standard highway cycle materially misstates it versus a long cruising scenario. That is an external validation of the assignment's decision to build a 500+ km corridor with sustained 2-3% grade plus a 6% mountain segment rather than scoring on a short cycle. It also establishes that 'electric-only at low speed/low power' is the conventional, published home for the electric machine — which is exactly the role S3 assigns its e-axle, and is the one part of S3 that is well-precedented.

items.name: Optimized Design and Analysis of a Series-Parallel Hybrid Electric Vehicle Powertrain for a Heavy Duty Truck
items.what_it_claims: Optimizes a series-parallel HEV powertrain for a heavy-duty truck and benchmarks it against a series HEV configuration on a highway drive cycle.
items.architecture: series-parallel vs series, heavy duty
items.quantified_result: Optimized series-parallel outperformed the series HEV in fuel economy by 20.99% on a highway drive cycle.
items.relevance_to_S3: A second independent confirmation, at a large magnitude, that a series path is the wrong architecture for highway-dominated heavy-duty duty. Bears directly on WS8's S1. Caution for WS8: 20.99% is a series-relative comparison, i.e. exactly the kind of self-referential baseline the assignment forbids ('every candidate is judged against S0, no self-referential comparisons') — cite it as evidence of the series penalty's direction and rough scale, never as an S3-style gain.

items.name: Design and performance analysis of hybrid electric Class 8 heavy-duty regional-haul trucks with a micro-pilot natural gas engine in real-world highway driving (Energy Conversion and Management, 2024, S0196890424003923)
items.what_it_claims: Builds a Class 8 Peterbilt baseline in Autonomie (Argonne, version AMBER-2022-U1) and evaluates hybrid electric regional-haul configurations under real-world highway conditions with a micro-pilot natural gas engine.
items.architecture: hybrid electric Class 8 regional-haul
items.quantified_result: Baseline modeling platform confirmed: Autonomie AMBER-2022-U1, Class 8 Peterbilt. Fuel-saving percentages NOT retrievable from accessible extracts.
items.relevance_to_S3: Most useful to WS8 as a methodology and provenance precedent rather than a result: it establishes Autonomie AMBER-2022-U1 + a named production tractor as the accepted way to construct a defensible Class 8 baseline in the recent peer-reviewed literature. WS8's S0 is being built independently, so this is the closest published analogue of the calibration WS8 must defend, and the paper is the best single target for a full-text follow-up when egress is restored.

items.name: Retrofit of a Heavy-Duty Diesel Truck: Comparison of Parallel and Series Hybrid Architectures with Waste Heat Recovery (SAE 2020-24-0015)
items.what_it_claims: Compares parallel and series hybrid retrofit architectures for a heavy-duty diesel truck with waste heat recovery included in the comparison.
items.architecture: parallel vs series retrofit + WHR, heavy-duty diesel
items.quantified_result: NONE FOUND — title and scope confirmed, results not retrievable without full text.
items.relevance_to_S3: The only source located that treats architecture choice and WHR as a single coupled decision, which is precisely the TASK 3 + TASK 4 coupling WS8 must resolve. Worth a full-text pull specifically to see whether the WHR benefit it reports is stated gross or net of the WHR system's own mass, since WS8's adoption gate (>=2.5% AFTER mass charge) turns entirely on that distinction.

items.name: Model-Based Optimization and Evaluation of Hybrid Powertrains for Commercial Heavy-Duty Class 8 Truck Applications (SAE 02-19-04-0025)
items.what_it_claims: Model-based optimization and evaluation across hybrid powertrain options for commercial Class 8 truck applications.
items.architecture: multiple hybrid architectures, Class 8
items.quantified_result: NONE FOUND — indexed and confirmed to exist; results not retrievable.
items.relevance_to_S3: Listed for completeness of the occupied-ground map. Its existence confirms that model-based architecture down-selection for Class 8 is a well-populated field, so WS8's TASK 3 is a re-run of an established exercise with two novel members (S2 cruise-lockup-with-disconnect, S3 tandem split), not a novel exercise.

items.name: Transmission speed and ratio optimization for heavy-duty electric truck (Heliyon 2022; ScienceDirect S2405844022013160; PMC9399168)
items.what_it_claims: Studies five transmission designs (2-speed single, 2+1 split, 2+2 split, 3-speed single, 4-speed single) with thousands of gear-ratio sets for a heavy-duty electric truck, against gradeability requirements. Finds a 3-speed single transmission meets gradeability with the lowest energy consumption and least complexity; also finds that increasing the gear count in a single transmission beats complex split arrangements because it holds the e-motors at higher-efficiency points.
items.architecture: multi-speed vs single-speed, heavy-duty battery-electric truck
items.quantified_result: 3-speed single transmission = lowest energy consumption meeting gradeability, among 2/2+1/2+2/3/4-speed candidates. Dual e-motor at matched speed: up to 5% benefit. Multi-speed reported elsewhere at 10-15% efficiency benefit for HD e-trucks (secondary claim, unverified source).
items.relevance_to_S3: Contradicting evidence against the transmission-deletion premise, and the strongest available on the electric side. The most gear-friendly modern application — a battery-electric heavy truck with a wide-constant-power machine, the case where single-speed should win if it ever wins — still optimizes to THREE ratios once real gradeability is imposed. S3 proposes fewer ratios than that on the harder side (a diesel with a ~1.8:1 usable speed band instead of a machine with a 3-4:1 constant-power band). Also directly relevant to S3's e-axle: WS8 should state whether the e-axle is single-speed, because this paper says a single-speed e-drive is not the energy optimum even when it is the only drive.

items.name: Simulation-Based Comparative Assessment of a Multi-Speed Transmission for an E-Retrofitted Heavy-Duty Truck (MDPI Energies 15(7) 2407, 2022; DOI 10.3390/en15072407)
items.what_it_claims: Assesses a multi-speed transmission for an electrically retrofitted heavy-duty truck. Finds multi-speed significantly improves traction performance and gradeability, while the effect on powertrain efficiency and energy consumption is 'rather minor'.
items.architecture: multi-speed vs single-speed, e-retrofit heavy-duty truck
items.quantified_result: Traction/gradeability: significant improvement. Powertrain efficiency and energy consumption: minor effect (no percentage retrievable).
items.relevance_to_S3: The cleanest published statement of why heavy trucks carry many ratios, and it is NOT the reason WS8 might assume. The gears exist for TRACTION AND GRADEABILITY, not for cruise efficiency. This reframes S3's whole case: deleting the gearbox costs little in steady cruise efficiency (S3's premise is defensible there) but attacks exactly the capability the gearbox is actually there to provide. WS8's TASK 5 S3-specific risks — fixed-ratio grade-hold floor, diesel-axle-only adhesion — are therefore not edge cases but the main event, and should be reported as the governing cases, not as sensitivities.

items.name: Torque fill-in for an automated shift manual transmission in a parallel hybrid electric vehicle (IEEE Xplore 1023222)
items.what_it_claims: Uses the hybrid electric machine to fill the torque gap between required (drive-cycle) torque and engine-provided torque during AMT gearshifts, especially upshifts, eliminating traction interruption and improving shift quality; the effect emulates the continuous torque of a torque-converter automatic.
items.architecture: P2/P3 parallel hybrid with AMT; electric torque fill during shifts
items.quantified_result: NONE FOUND as a fuel percentage — the published benefit is driveability/shift quality (elimination of torque interruption), not a quantified fuel saving. Related HD figure located: a two-motor powertrain for extended-range electric buses reduced electric consumption 8.6% and fuel consumption 9.1% vs conventional (different architecture, not a torque-fill attribution).
items.relevance_to_S3: This is the occupied-ground boundary for WS8's core program premise, and it cuts against the strong form of that premise. Every located torque-fill paper fills gaps in a transmission that still exists; none deletes the gearbox. The published benefit is driveability, not fuel. So the Vehicle Zero premise as restated in BASELINE_v3 ('electric torque-fill replaces the gearbox') has no external quantified support at Class 8 scale — WS8 should not import an assumed fuel credit for torque fill into S2 or S3, and should state explicitly that the credit is zero unless its own model produces one.

items.name: EPA Greenhouse gas Emissions Model (GEM), Phase 2 — v3.x / v4.0, EPA-420-B-16-067 and successors; 40 CFR 1037.520
items.what_it_claims: The regulatory compliance simulation for Class 7/8 combination tractors under the US HD GHG Phase 2 rule. Fixes vehicle-level modeling parameters (efficiencies, accessory powers) across all tractor types; accepts OEM-specified CdA by aerodynamic bin and OEM-specified Crr separately for steer and drive axles; permits OEM axle efficiency maps, transmission efficiency maps and torque converter capacity factors to replace GEM defaults.
items.architecture: conventional Class 7/8 combination tractor (regulatory reference model)
items.quantified_result: Heavy-haul tractor default CdA = 5.0 m^2. From MY2027, GEM internally subtracts 0.3 m^2 from a high-roof tractor's CdA input to represent an improved box trailer with rear fairing. Crr is OEM-specified per axle in Phase 2 (no single default retrievable). Axle efficiency up to 97% cited as achievable with advanced low-viscosity lubricants.
items.relevance_to_S3: The defensible citation anchor for WS8's CdA and for the assignment's provisional 5.5 m^2. Note the direction of the evidence: the regulatory HEAVY-HAUL default is 5.0 m^2, and MY2027 high-roof tractors get a further 0.3 m^2 credit, so 5.5 m^2 sits at the conservative (draggier) end of the modern regulatory range rather than mid-band. WS8 should either hold 5.5 m^2 and label it conservative-provisional, or run the CdA sensitivity — note that in Vehicle Zero's G1 record CdA 5.4 was the sole break-even condition (BASELINE_v3), so CdA is a known hinge parameter in this program and deserves an explicit case in the R14 export rather than a single point value.

items.name: 40 CFR 1037.528 — Coastdown procedures for calculating drag area (CdA); and 40 CFR 1037.525 aerodynamic measurements for tractors
items.what_it_claims: Defines the regulatory coastdown determination of CdA for a tractor tested with a standard trailer. Total road-load force from measured deceleration comprises aerodynamic drag, rolling resistance, axle spin losses and road grade; the speed dependence of drive-axle losses and tire rolling resistance is separately quantified to isolate the aerodynamic term; CdA is estimated at the observed yaw angle per run. Test tires must be SmartWay-verified or have Crr at or below 5.1 kg/metric ton.
items.architecture: conventional tractor-trailer, regulatory test procedure
items.quantified_result: Coastdown test-tire requirement: Crr <= 5.1 kg/tonne (i.e. Crr <= 0.0051) or SmartWay-verified. Road-load decomposition explicitly includes axle spin losses as a distinct term from rolling resistance.
items.relevance_to_S3: Two things WS8 needs. First, a citable floor for Crr: the regulator's own test-tire threshold is 0.0051, which makes the assignment's provisional 0.0055 a defensible loaded-combination value rather than an optimistic one. Second, and more important for S3: the regulation treats AXLE SPIN LOSS as a first-class road-load term separate from rolling resistance. S3 has a disconnectable e-axle and a declutchable diesel axle, so its spin-drag bookkeeping is the crux of the design, and this citation establishes that spin drag is a real, separately-measured quantity — the same member that cost the Vehicle Zero locked path 1.77 pp in the G1 attribution. S3 must show both G1 taxes deleted by construction, and this is the standard against which 'deleted' has to be argued.

items.name: EPA SmartWay verified low rolling resistance tire program — Crr target values (SAE J1269 / ISO 28580)
items.what_it_claims: Sets rolling-resistance coefficient target values a tire model must meet, by wheel position, to earn SmartWay verification, using SAE J1269 or ISO 28580.
items.architecture: tractor-trailer tires by axle position
items.quantified_result: SmartWay Crr targets, kg force per metric ton (J1269): steer 6.6, drive 7.0, trailer 5.5.
items.relevance_to_S3: Gives WS8 a per-axle basis for a combination-weighted Crr instead of a single asserted scalar. DERIVED from these targets at the standard US bridge-formula axle split (steer 5,443 kg / drive tandem 15,422 kg / trailer tandem 15,422 kg): load-weighted Crr = (5443*6.6 + 15422*7.0 + 15422*5.5)/36287 = 6.32 kg/t = 0.0063. That is 15% ABOVE the assignment's provisional 0.0055. So 0.0055 is not a mid-band SmartWay fleet value — it is a best-in-class value that presumes better-than-verification-threshold tires on every position. WS8 should either state that assumption explicitly or carry 0.0055 / 0.0063 as an enumerated case pair in the R14 export, since a 15% Crr error moves rolling drag by ~8 kW at 100 km/h (DERIVED), roughly 6% of total wheel power, which is twice the ADVANCE margin.

items.name: NHTSA / Southwest Research Institute Phase 2 engine fuel maps — public Excel release (Detroit DD15 14.8 L base map; 12.3 L delta maps; Cummins 6.7 L / 4.5 L; Ford 3.5 L V6, 6.2 L V8)
items.what_it_claims: NHTSA released, as Microsoft Excel files, the SwRI engine maps used in research supporting the NPRM for the EPA/NHTSA Phase 2 heavy-duty GHG and fuel-efficiency standards — specifically those where GT-POWER simulation and experimental validation were completed entirely with Federal funding. Includes a Detroit 14.8 L DD15 base map plus a 12.3 L variant delta map, and a separate 'DD15 Fuel Maps (Percent Change Relative To Baseline)' spreadsheet.
items.architecture: engine fuel/BSFC maps for HD diesel, 12.3 L and 14.8 L class
items.quantified_result: Publicly downloadable Excel fuel maps for a 14.8 L DD15 (base) and 12.3 L variant (delta). This is the ONLY located public, machine-readable, 11-15 L class HD diesel map that is federally funded and unrestricted. Peak BSFC value not retrievable from search extracts — must be read from the spreadsheet.
items.relevance_to_S3: This is the answer to WS8 TASK 2's map requirement and it should be the S0 map of record. It satisfies the program's provenance discipline in a way a digitized contour plot never can: federally funded, publicly released, machine-readable, experimentally validated, and in exactly the 12.3-14.8 L band the assignment specifies for a ~330-370 kW 13 L-class engine. The 12.3 L delta map additionally gives WS8 a CITED basis for S3's 'engine downsized toward cruise-plus-margin' rather than an invented scaling law — which matters because BASELINE_v3's G1 attribution shows a map-vs-scalar swap moved the answer by 7.01 pp (R12). Retrieve both spreadsheets and pin them by SHA before any S0 run.

items.name: Cummins / Ram ISB Diesel Engine Fuel Maps Spreadsheet (NHTSA public document)
items.what_it_claims: Publicly posted spreadsheet of fuel maps for the Cummins ISB diesel. A MY2013 Cummins ISB 6.7 L was tested to characterize the fueling map and energy audit of a US EPA 2010-compliant medium-duty diesel engine; the stated purpose of such work is to develop Autonomie fuel-map inputs (fuel rate looked up on speed and torque) for EPA-2010-compliant heavy- and medium-duty diesels.
items.architecture: map-based engine model input, medium-duty diesel
items.quantified_result: Cummins ISB 6.7 L, MY2013, EPA-2010 compliant. Map is fuel rate vs speed and torque (Autonomie lookup convention). Peak BSFC not retrievable from extracts.
items.relevance_to_S3: Wrong displacement for WS8's 13 L-class S0 (6.7 L is medium-duty), so it is NOT the map of record — but it is the reference for the FORM Autonomie expects: a speed-torque fuel-rate lookup, not a BSFC scalar with a part-load correction. That form matters to WS8 because it is the same distinction that produced R12's 7.01 pp swing in Vehicle Zero. Use this to justify the map convention; use the DD15 map for the numbers.

items.name: Heavy-duty vehicle diesel engine efficiency evaluation and energy audit (WVU for ICCT, October 2014)
items.what_it_claims: Independent test-cell evaluation and energy audit of US heavy-duty diesel engines, characterizing fueling maps and efficiency for EPA-2010-compliant engines. Cited engines include a Cummins ISM heavy-duty diesel with the ECM set to 400 hp / 1250 lb-ft.
items.architecture: conventional HD diesel engine characterization
items.quantified_result: Cummins ISM test point: 400 hp (298 kW), 1250 lb-ft (1695 Nm). Peak BSFC / BTE values not retrievable from extracts.
items.relevance_to_S3: The standard independent (non-OEM, non-regulatory) cross-check on HD diesel efficiency, and the right document to use to sanity-check whatever peak BSFC the DD15 spreadsheet yields. Worth a full-text pull for its energy audit, which decomposes where the fuel energy goes — WS8 owes WS6 a rejected-heat ledger by component and case (program rule 7), and this audit is the published template for that decomposition on a 13 L-class engine.

items.name: Diesel Engine Characterization and Performance Scaling via Brake Specific Fuel Consumption Map Dimensional Analysis (ASME DSCC 2019, V002T11A003; OSTI 1561789)
items.what_it_claims: Applies dimensional analysis to heavy-duty truck engine maps to produce a single dimensionless, uniformly applicable BSFC map that fits a wide range of diesel engines, enabling engine performance comparison and fuel-efficient matching of engines to loads and routes. Commonality emerges when engine data is scaled by dimensional parameters chosen to align the primary operating points across engines.
items.architecture: engine map scaling methodology, HD diesel
items.quantified_result: The dimensionless engine map fits the minimum-BSFC regions of four diesel engines to within 2.5%.
items.relevance_to_S3: This is the citable scaling law WS8 needs for TASK 3's downsized S3 engine, and it comes with an error bar. The assignment requires stated scaling laws for electric components (from WS2 r4) but leaves the engine-side scaling for S3's downsizing unstated; this paper supplies it and bounds it at 2.5% in the min-BSFC region. Two cautions for WS8: 2.5% is comparable to the entire 3% ADVANCE margin, so the scaling error must be carried as an explicit uncertainty on S3 rather than absorbed silently; and the fit is validated in the MINIMUM-BSFC region, which is precisely where a downsized cruise-optimized engine is supposed to live but is NOT where S3's engine operates at band edges — so the 2.5% figure does not cover S3's off-point excursions.

items.name: Reported minimum BSFC of mainstream heavy-duty truck diesels; Detroit DD15 and DOE SuperTruck peak brake thermal efficiency
items.what_it_claims: Industry/technical reporting of the efficiency ceiling for volume-production heavy-duty truck diesels and for the DOE SuperTruck demonstrator engines.
items.architecture: conventional HD diesel, 13-15 L class
items.quantified_result: Lowest BSFC of mainstream HD truck diesels in volume commercial use: 182 g/kWh, corresponding to 46% brake thermal efficiency. Detroit DD15 claimed peak BTE >48%. Detroit SuperTruck demonstrated 48.1% BTE = 46.8% engine + 1.3% waste heat recovery, with hardware in hand for 50% BTE.
items.relevance_to_S3: The peak-BSFC anchor for TASK 2 and a hard sanity bound. WS8's S0 map must have a minimum BSFC in the 182-195 g/kWh region for a modern 13 L-class engine; a map bottoming out much below 182 g/kWh is not a production engine and the calibration is wrong. Note the SuperTruck decomposition is directly load-bearing for TASK 4: Detroit's WHR contributed only 1.3 percentage points of BTE out of 48.1 (2.7% relative), which is at or below WS8's pre-committed >=2.5% net adoption gate BEFORE any mass charge is applied. That is the single most important external number for the WHR decision.

items.name: ICCT / TUV NORD fuel consumption and emissions testing of tractor-trailers in the European Union and the United States (2018)
items.what_it_claims: Chassis/track testing of three tractor-trailers — a typical EU tractor-trailer, a best-in-class EU tractor-trailer, and a best-in-class US tractor-trailer — over the drive cycles and payloads stipulated by the EU CO2 certification regulation (VECTO) and by US HDV fuel consumption standards.
items.architecture: conventional diesel tractor-trailer (EU and US)
items.quantified_result: Typical EU tractor-trailer: 32.6 L/100 km over the regulatory Long Haul cycle. Best-in-class EU tractor-trailer: 29.9 L/100 km (typical is 9% higher). Separately reported: 33.1 L/100 km over the Long Haul cycle at the regulatory payload of 19.3 tonnes.
items.relevance_to_S3: The single best public reference band for WS8 TASK 2, and it lands squarely inside the assignment's 30-38 L/100 km sanity corridor. Both cycle and payload are stated, which is what makes it usable: VECTO Long Haul, 19.3 t payload. Caveat WS8 must state: EU Group 5 4x2 tractor-semitrailer at ~40 t GCW regulatory maximum is not identical to a US 6x4 at 36.3 t GCW — the EU vehicle is heavier and typically speed-limited to 85-90 km/h, while WS8's corridor runs 85-105 km/h. Use 32.6-33.1 L/100 km as the anchor, and state the GCW and speed-band deltas as named adjustments rather than assuming transferability.

items.name: VECTO regulatory payloads and cycle definitions (EU HDV CO2 certification; Group 5 tractor-semitrailer)
items.what_it_claims: Defines the EU certification cycles (Urban Delivery, Regional Delivery, Long Haul) and the payloads at which fuel consumption and CO2 are declared for each vehicle group. Group 5 = tractor chassis, 4x2 axle configuration.
items.architecture: conventional tractor-semitrailer, regulatory reference
items.quantified_result: Declared payloads: 12.9 tonnes representative for Urban Delivery and Regional Delivery; 19.3 tonnes representative for Long Haul; 25.6 tonnes full payload. Results also declared empty.
items.relevance_to_S3: Supplies the payload denominators WS8's metric of record requires. WS8 judges candidates on fuel energy per PAYLOAD tonne-km, so every reference band imported from the literature must arrive with its payload attached or it cannot be converted into the metric — this standard is what makes the 32.6 and 33.1 L/100 km figures usable rather than decorative. The 12.9 / 19.3 / 25.6 t triple also maps cleanly onto the assignment's TASK 5 payload +/-20% sensitivity, giving WS8 a regulator-sanctioned rather than invented payload spread.

items.name: NACFE Run on Less (2017) and Annual Fleet Fuel Study (2022-2023) — real-world US Class 8 fuel economy benchmarks
items.what_it_claims: Run on Less: seven US Class 8 tractors from seven fleets driven in real freight service over 17 days. Annual Fleet Fuel Study: tracks 14 participating fleets' adoption of efficiency technologies and their realized fuel economy against the national average.
items.architecture: conventional diesel Class 8 tractor-trailer, real-world on-road
items.quantified_result: Run on Less 2017: 10.1 mpg average across 7 trucks over 17 days, against a stated US over-the-road tractor-trailer national average of 6.4 mpg. Fleet Fuel Study: participant average 7.62 mpg (2022), 7.77 mpg (2023); stated national average 6.9 mpg. DERIVED conversions at 235.215/mpg: 10.1 mpg = 23.3 L/100 km; 7.77 mpg = 30.3 L/100 km; 7.62 mpg = 30.9 L/100 km; 6.9 mpg = 34.1 L/100 km; 6.4 mpg = 36.8 L/100 km.
items.relevance_to_S3: This is the US-side reference band, and it brackets the assignment's 30-38 L/100 km corridor almost exactly: the US national average (6.4-6.9 mpg = 36.8-34.1 L/100 km) sits at the corridor's upper edge and the best-practice fleet average (7.62-7.77 mpg = 30.9-30.3 L/100 km) sits at its lower edge. So the corridor as written spans 'US fleet average' to 'US best-practice fleet', which is the right target for a modern S0. Critical exclusion: 10.1 mpg (23.3 L/100 km) falls BELOW the corridor and must NOT be used to calibrate S0 — Run on Less trucks were aero-optimized, driver-optimized and not uniformly loaded to 36.3 t GCW. Calibrating a loaded 36.3 t S0 to 10.1 mpg would understate S0 fuel by ~25% and would silently inflate every candidate's percentage gain against it.

items.name: Coca-Cola Refreshments Class 8 Diesel Electric Hybrid Tractor Evaluation: 13-Month Final Report (NREL/TP-5600-53502, 2012)
items.what_it_claims: 13-month in-service evaluation of five Kenworth T370 hybrid Class 8 tractors against five Freightliner M2106 conventional diesel tractors in Coca-Cola Refreshments delivery service in Miami, Florida, plus chassis dynamometer testing over multiple drive cycles.
items.architecture: parallel diesel-electric hybrid Class 8 (delivery/vocational duty)
items.quantified_result: On-road: 13.7% higher fuel economy than conventional; 12% lower fuel cost per mile. Chassis dyno: up to 30% fuel economy improvement depending on drive cycle; up to 32.1% improvement in ton-miles per gallon.
items.relevance_to_S3: The best available measured (not simulated) Class 8 hybrid result, and the sharpest illustration of the duty-cycle dependence WS8 must respect. The gap between 13.7% real-world and up-to-30% on a favorable dyno cycle is the size of the error a cycle choice can introduce — larger than WS8's entire ADVANCE margin, several times over. Note the duty: Miami beverage delivery is stop-start vocational work, the regime where hybrids win. It is NOT WS8's line-haul corridor, and the 13.7% must not be read across to TASK 1(a). It is, however, a fair external reference point for TASK 1(b)'s regional mixed cycle, and the ton-miles-per-gallon metric (32.1%) is the closest published analogue to WS8's fuel-per-payload-tonne-km metric of record.

items.name: 21st Century Truck Partnership / National Academies reviews — Class 8 tractor-trailer energy audit and driveline goals
items.what_it_claims: DOE-industry partnership and its National Academies reviews establish the reference energy audit for a Class 8 tractor-trailer and set technology goals for aerodynamic drag, rolling resistance and driveline losses.
items.architecture: conventional Class 8 tractor-trailer (reference energy accounting)
items.quantified_result: Energy audit of dissipative losses: 60% engine, 21% aerodynamic, 13% rolling resistance, 6% drivetrain + auxiliary. Aerodynamic and rolling resistance together consume 60-85% of total power depending on speed. Aero goal: reduce Class 8 tractor-trailer drag 20%, Cd 0.69 -> 0.55. Driveline goal: reduce powertrain and driveline losses by 50%. Axle efficiency up to 97% cited as achievable with advanced low-viscosity lubricants. Also cited: 1.5% fuel economy improvement per 1,000 lb (454 kg) of weight reduction.
items.relevance_to_S3: Three things WS8 needs. (1) The 6% drivetrain+auxiliary share is the citable basis for the assignment's required 'transmission and axle efficiencies stated' — a combined driveline efficiency near 0.94-0.95 is consistent with it, and 97% single-axle efficiency bounds the optimistic end. (2) The Cd 0.69 baseline, at a typical Class 8 frontal area near 10 m^2, implies a baseline CdA near 6.9 m^2 and an improved-target CdA near 5.5 m^2 — which independently supports the assignment's provisional 5.5 m^2 as a modern-aero rather than legacy value. (3) The 1.5% per 1,000 lb sensitivity is the direct conversion factor WS8 needs to charge hybrid mass against fuel, and is a useful cross-check on the payload-tonne-km metric: a 1,000 kg powertrain mass penalty is worth roughly 3.3% fuel, i.e. more than the entire ADVANCE margin, which is exactly why the assignment made payload the denominator.

items.name: Heavy-duty electric turbocompound — NESCCAF/ICCT, Caterpillar, John Deere, Volvo D13TC, and the electric turbocompounding literature
items.what_it_claims: Recovers exhaust energy through a power turbine coupled to a generator (electric) or geared to the crank (mechanical), returning energy electrically or mechanically rather than as shaft-only compounding.
items.architecture: exhaust energy recovery bolted to a conventional HD diesel
items.quantified_result: Electric turbocompound claimed as large as 10% fuel consumption reduction; NESCCAF/ICCT estimated 4.2% INCLUDING accessory electrification; Caterpillar modeled 3-5%; John Deere investigated a system offering 10%. Volvo D13TC / MD13TC / D12 500TC with axial turbines: 3% efficiency improvement. Electric turbocompounding research: up to 15.8 kW from a low-pressure-ratio turbine, up to 4% BSFC improvement. Modeling of promising turbine combinations: 1-4% BSFC at high load, 5-6% at peak power. MASS: NONE FOUND in any accessible source.
items.relevance_to_S3: Feeds TASK 4 directly, and the honest reading is unfavorable to adoption. The credible independent estimates cluster at 3-4.2% GROSS (Volvo's production figure is 3%; ICCT's is 4.2% and that number already includes accessory electrification, so the turbocompound-only share is lower). WS8's gate is >=2.5% NET of mass charge. With gross benefit at 3-4% and no published mass figure to charge against it, the margin between gross benefit and the gate is under 1.5 percentage points — smaller than the uncertainty in the benefit itself. Also note the 5-6% figures are AT PEAK POWER, which is not where a line-haul engine lives; the 1-4% at high load is the relevant band, and S3's downsized cruise-optimized engine would sit near the bottom of it. WS8 should carry the mass as an explicit unknown and report the gate result as mass-conditional.

items.name: Organic Rankine Cycle waste heat recovery for heavy-duty truck engines — Cummins SuperTruck, PACCAR/Cummins, and the ORC review literature
items.what_it_claims: Bottoming cycle recovering exhaust, EGR, charge-air and coolant heat through an organic working fluid and expander, returning power mechanically or as electricity. Cummins' SuperTruck implementation collected heat from charge air, EGR cooler, engine coolant and exhaust, delivering roughly 5 kWe.
items.architecture: ORC bottoming cycle on a conventional HD diesel
items.quantified_result: Cummins SuperTruck: 3.6% brake thermal efficiency increase; WHR system claimed to reduce fuel consumption up to 6%. ORC reviews: 4.48-7.52% truck fuel economy improvement, 7.52% maximum at full load. One HD system: 3.8% (coolant + EGR), rising to 7.5% with raised coolant temperature and additional heat sources. Projected BTE improvement generally 2-4% depending on heat source content. Component mass: a scroll expander derived from an air scroll compressor, 122 cm^3 displacement, weighs 10.4 kg (component only, not system). FULL SYSTEM MASS: NONE FOUND. PACCAR/Cummins conclusion: 'for optimum freight efficiency, the fuel savings under transient conditions don't outweigh the additional weight, and impact on aerodynamics.'
items.relevance_to_S3: The PACCAR/Cummins sentence is the most important single finding for TASK 4 and it is a qualitative prior kill. Two OEMs that actually built and ran ORC on trucks concluded the mass and aero penalty exceeds the transient fuel saving for freight efficiency — which is WS8's own metric, fuel per payload tonne-km, stated in industry language. The gross numbers look comfortably above the 2.5% gate (3.6-7.5%), but every one of them is gross, the only mass datum found is a 10.4 kg component inside a system that also needs a boiler, recuperator, condenser, pump, working fluid and added cooling capacity, and the highest figures are at FULL LOAD or with raised coolant temperature. WS8 should treat the pre-committed gate as likely to fail on mass, run it honestly, and report the mass assumption as the governing uncertainty — dropping it 'without ceremony' as the assignment provides, rather than defending it.

items.name: Hyliion 6X4HE hybrid electric drive axle (Class 8 e-axle overlay product)
items.what_it_claims: An electrified 6x4 drive axle replacing one axle of the tandem on a conventional Class 8 tractor, adding regenerative braking and electric assist while leaving the diesel engine and its transmission in place. Marketed as capturing power on deceleration and applying electric power to hold the diesel near its efficient speed.
items.architecture: through-the-road / P4-style e-axle overlay on an otherwise unmodified conventional diesel driveline (transmission RETAINED)
items.quantified_result: Up to 15% fuel savings from the hybrid drive alone, in its optimum operating environment, stated as rolling hilly terrain. Marketed 30% total is a blend of three separate technologies: 15% electric hybrid + 12% APU (idle reduction) + 3% aerodynamics. Battery kWh, motor kW and system mass: NONE FOUND in accessible sources.
items.relevance_to_S3: The closest commercial analogue to S3's axle B, and the most direct contradiction of S3's axle A. Hyliion occupies the tandem-split e-axle ground that S3 proposes — but it keeps the diesel's multi-speed transmission entirely intact and never touches the ICE ratio. So the e-axle-owns-regen-and-assist half of S3 is occupied ground with a commercial product behind it; the delete-the-gearbox half has no product, no program and no paper. WS8 should also note the marketing decomposition: only 15 of the headline 30 points are hybrid, and that 15% is qualified to rolling hilly terrain — the terrain where the ORNL simulation work also finds hybrid benefit concentrates. On flat line-haul the honest expectation is well below 15%.

items.name: Revoy electric dolly (Class 8 hybrid retrofit via a powered dolly between tractor and trailer)
items.what_it_claims: A quick-attach electric dolly with its own motor and battery pack inserted between tractor and trailer, driving through its own powered axle to assist the diesel tractor, with battery swapping along the route. Requires no modification to the tractor's engine or driveline.
items.architecture: through-the-road hybrid via an independently powered intermediate axle; tractor driveline and transmission entirely unmodified
items.quantified_result: 575 kWh battery (800 kWh version announced); approximately 200 miles (322 km) of electric assist for an 80,000 lb (36,287 kg) combination. Claimed fuel economy shift from 6-8 mpg to 20-35 mpg with emissions cut 70-90%; 85% emissions cut cited for the 575 kWh plug-in module; over $5,000 per truck annual savings.
items.relevance_to_S3: Occupied ground for through-the-road electrification, and a caution about how such claims are constructed. The 20-35 mpg figure is not a powertrain efficiency result — it is diesel-only fuel divided by distance while grid electricity does most of the work, so it measures fuel substitution, not fuel efficiency. WS8's metric of record (fuel ENERGY per payload tonne-km) with an honest energy accounting for the electrical input will not reproduce anything like it. The genuinely relevant datum is the mass and payload consequence: a 575 kWh pack plus dolly structure is a very large payload displacement at a fixed 36,300 kg GCW, which is exactly the tax WS8's denominator is designed to expose and which none of Revoy's public figures charge.

items.name: Heavy-duty transmission ratio-spread, startability and gradeability practice (12-speed and 18-speed AMT specification literature)
items.what_it_claims: Establishes why heavy trucks carry 12-18 ratios: the transmission must provide a low gear for startability and low-speed operation and a high top gear for highway cruise. Startability is the ability to launch on a grade; gradeability is the maximum grade at which traction still moves the truck forward. Aggressive downspeeding with direct-drive transmissions (2.15-2.47/2.64 axle ratios) is explicitly limited to long-haul operators spending 80-90% of time in the top two gears with at least 30 miles between stops.
items.architecture: conventional multi-speed AMT/manual, Class 8
items.quantified_result: 18-speed manuals offer 12-14:1 low ratios paired with 3.55-4.10 axles. A DD15 at 1,850 lb-ft through a 12:1 transmission low and a 4:1 axle exceeds 50,000 lb-ft at the tires. Kenworth recommends 15-20% startability for most heavy-haul applications. 12-speed AMTs now handle ratings mostly exceeding 2,050 lb-ft. Mid-weight market 47,000-57,000 kg opening to 12-speed alongside traditional 18-speed.
items.relevance_to_S3: The quantified statement of what S3 proposes to delete. Production practice provides ~50,000 lb-ft at the tires through a 12:1 low; S3 provides ONE ratio on the diesel path and hands the entire launch and low-speed duty to the e-axle. That is not necessarily wrong — but it means the e-axle must independently satisfy the 15-20% startability specification at 36,300 kg GCW, alone, with no torque multiplication available from the diesel path, and must do so on a depleted battery. WS8 must state S3's startability in the same units the industry uses and show it met at the SOC floor, or S3 has no launch capability at all in the case that matters. Note also the downspeeding qualifier: even direct-drive downspeeding is restricted to 80-90% top-two-gear duty with 30+ mile stop spacing, i.e. the industry already treats a NARROWED ratio set as acceptable only in the narrowest slice of line-haul duty. S3 narrows it to one.

items.name: Engine downspeeding fuel sensitivity (heavy-duty line-haul practice)
items.what_it_claims: Industry-standard rule of thumb, consistently reported across independent sources, relating cruise engine speed to fuel consumption in Class 8 line-haul: roughly 1% fuel economy improvement per 100 rpm reduction in cruise engine speed. Fast axle ratios (2.47, 2.28) with direct-drive transmissions are the preferred long-haul strategy.
items.architecture: conventional Class 8 line-haul, downsped
items.quantified_result: ~1% fuel economy per 100 rpm of cruise engine speed reduction. Aggressive downspeeding axle ratios 2.15-2.47/2.64 (direct drive); a 2.47 axle burns measurably less at speed than a 3.55.
items.relevance_to_S3: The conversion factor that prices S3's fixed-ratio penalty across the speed band, and it is a real tax that S3 cannot escape by construction. DERIVED: with one ratio sized to 1,200 rpm at 100 km/h, the assignment's 85-105 km/h corridor forces engine speed from 1,020 to 1,260 rpm — a 240 rpm excursion, worth ~2.4% fuel at this sensitivity, against an ADVANCE margin of 3%. A multi-ratio AMT holds cruise rpm nearly constant across that same band by shifting; S3 cannot. WS8 must charge this explicitly as an S3 off-point tax (the assignment already requires exactly this for S2 at band edges — the same charge applies to S3 across the whole corridor, not just at edges) and must not assume the fixed ratio sits at the BSFC optimum everywhere in the speed band.

items.name: NREL FASTSim (Future Automotive Systems Technology Simulator) and FASTSim Vehicle Database
items.what_it_claims: Open-source NREL vehicle simulation tool for evaluating technology effects on efficiency and performance, covering light-duty, two-wheelers and medium- and heavy-duty vocational vehicles, with a public prebuilt vehicle database on GitHub.
items.architecture: vehicle-level simulation framework, multiple powertrains
items.quantified_result: Confirmed accessible and open (the only host reachable from this environment). Vehicle file parameter schema verified directly from a retrieved file: drag coefficient, frontal area (m^2), wheel rolling resistance coefficient, transmission efficiency, fuel converter max power (kW), fuel converter base weight (kg), glider weight (kg), wheel radius (m). No Class 8 tractor file located; the reachable example was a light-duty vehicle (drag coeff 0.393, frontal area 2.12 m^2, wheel rr coeff 0.007, transmission efficiency 0.875).
items.relevance_to_S3: Useful to WS8 in two narrow ways only. First, it is a reachable, open, citable precedent for the PARAMETER SET a defensible road-load model must declare — the assignment requires stated efficiencies and cited road-load values, and this schema is the published list of what 'stated' means. Second, its medium/heavy-duty coverage is vocational, not line-haul tractor, so it is NOT a source for WS8's S0 numbers. Do not calibrate against it; use the DD15 map and the ICCT/NACFE bands.

contradictions.claim: S3's premise that a diesel axle can drive a 36.3 t Class 8 combination through ONE fixed ratio is contradicted by the engine's own usable speed band: one ratio buys only a ~1.8:1 road-speed window, leaving the diesel axle dead across most of the corridor.
contradictions.evidence: A modern HD diesel's usable driving band runs roughly 1,000 rpm (peak torque) to 1,800 rpm (rated) — about 1.80:1. With a single ratio, road speed range equals engine speed range exactly. DERIVED, sized three ways: (a) 105 km/h at rated 1,800 rpm puts 1,000 rpm at 58.3 km/h, so the diesel axle is DEAD below 58.3 km/h; (b) sized for modern downsped cruise, 1,200 rpm at 100 km/h, 1,000 rpm falls at 83.3 km/h — dead below 83.3 km/h, and 1,800 rpm would correspond to an unusable 150 km/h; (c) 105 km/h at 1,400 rpm leaves it dead below 75.0 km/h. There is no sizing that both reaches 105 km/h and covers low speed. The literature independently confirms the mechanism from the other direction: heavy trucks carry 12-18 ratios with 12-14:1 lows precisely because 'the transmission needs a good overall ratio range with a low gear for low speed operation and startability as well as a high top gear for highway speeds', and even the mildest published narrowing — direct-drive downspeeding — is restricted to operators spending 80-90% of time in the top two gears with 30+ miles between stops.

contradictions.claim: S3's 'engine downsized toward cruise-plus-margin' cannot survive the assignment's own 6% mountain segment: at the speeds a loaded 36.3 t combination actually climbs a 6% grade, the fixed-ratio diesel axle is below its speed floor and disconnected, so the e-axle must carry the entire climb alone — at full engine-class power.
contradictions.evidence: DERIVED at 36,300 kg, CdA 5.5 m^2, Crr 0.0055, rho 1.184: wheel power on a 6% grade is 196.3 kW at 30 km/h, 263.6 kW at 40 km/h, 332.7 kW at 50 km/h and 389.4 kW at 58 km/h. With the diesel axle sized to reach 105 km/h at rated speed it is dead below 58.3 km/h (see previous finding), so every one of those points is e-axle-only. Energy, DERIVED at 50 km/h: a 10 km / 600 m-rise 6% climb needs 66.5 kWh at the wheels (59.4 potential + 5.4 rolling + 1.7 aero); 15 km / 900 m needs 99.8 kWh; 20 km / 1,200 m needs 133.1 kWh — roughly 74-148 kWh from the battery at ~90% e-driveline efficiency, for ONE climb, with no engine contribution to recharge during it. This inverts S3's sizing logic twice over: the e-axle must be rated at full tractive power (not 'peak assist'), and the pack must be sized for a mountain climb (not as a buffer). For scale, Vehicle Zero's ratified pack is 11.08 kWh usable (BASELINE_v3) — the S3 mountain requirement is 7-13x that.

contradictions.claim: S3's tandem split creates a diesel-axle-only adhesion failure on exactly the cruise grades the assignment names, because driving one axle of the tandem halves the normal load available to react tractive force.
contradictions.evidence: DERIVED at the standard US bridge-formula split (steer 5,443 kg / drive tandem 15,422 kg / trailer tandem 15,422 kg = 36,287 kg): a single driven axle of the tandem carries 7,711 kg, only 21.3% of GCW. Required adhesion coefficient with the full tandem driven vs one axle driven: 2% grade at 85 km/h, 0.072 vs 0.144; 3% at 85 km/h, 0.096 vs 0.191; 3% at 60 km/h, 0.090 vs 0.179; 6% at 40 km/h, 0.157 vs 0.314; 6% at 60 km/h, 0.160 vs 0.321. Against reference adhesion (dry asphalt 0.7-0.8, wet 0.4-0.6, packed snow 0.2-0.3, ice ~0.1), the single-driven-axle case REQUIRES 0.31-0.33 on a 6% grade — which exceeds packed snow entirely and leaves no margin. The full-tandem case (0.157-0.166) passes packed snow comfortably. This is a failure created by S3's architecture, not by the grade. It is the assignment's own TASK 5 risk 'diesel-axle-only adhesion on cruise grades', and the numbers say it is a real limit, not a theoretical one. Mitigation exists (the e-axle drives the other tandem axle, restoring combined adhesion) but it is available only while the battery holds charge — so adhesion and the mountain-climb energy finding above fail together, in the same conditions, on the same corner.

contradictions.claim: Whenever S3's fixed-ratio diesel axle is out of band, S3 degenerates into a series/battery path and inherits the documented series double-conversion penalty that makes series hybrids net-negative on Class 8 line-haul.
contradictions.evidence: ORNL (SAE 2014-01-2326) measured component energy losses across architectures on Class 8 trucks: motor + generator loss 7.4% for series against 1.0% for parallel and 0.8% for dual-mode, concluding series is 'absolutely negative' for long-haul fuel economy because of the dual-step mechanical-electrical-mechanical conversion, and 'not attractive for Class 8 trucks, especially at high vehicle speeds'. The companion ORNL study (TRR 2502, 2015; 15 L 2010-compliant diesel, freeway-dominated cycle) found parallel and dual-mode both delivered 7-8% while series showed 'no significant fuel economy benefit'. An independent optimization study found a series-parallel powertrain beat a series one by 20.99% on a highway cycle. S3 is nominally a parallel/through-the-road architecture and should escape this penalty — but only in the speed window where its diesel axle is actually connected. Below that window (58.3-83.3 km/h depending on ratio sizing, DERIVED above) all tractive power routes through the battery and e-axle, which is a series path with an added battery round-trip loss on top of the 7.4%. WS8 must therefore compute S3's connected-fraction over each cycle and charge the series penalty on the remainder; assuming parallel-path efficiency across the whole corridor would overstate S3.

contradictions.claim: S3's fixed ratio cannot hold the engine at its best cruise point across the assignment's own 85-105 km/h corridor, and the resulting off-optimum tax is comparable to the entire ADVANCE margin.
contradictions.evidence: The heavy-duty line-haul sensitivity reported consistently across independent industry sources is ~1% fuel economy per 100 rpm of cruise engine speed change. DERIVED: with one ratio sized to 1,200 rpm at 100 km/h, the corridor's 85-105 km/h span forces engine speed from 1,020 to 1,260 rpm — a 240 rpm excursion worth roughly 2.4% fuel, against WS8's pre-committed >=3% ADVANCE bar. A multi-ratio AMT holds cruise rpm nearly flat across the same band by shifting; a single ratio cannot. The assignment already requires S2 to 'charge every remaining tax honestly (re-derive drag when connected, off-point engine operation at band edges)' — this finding says the identical charge is owed by S3, and not merely at band edges but continuously across the corridor, because S3 has no ratio to shift to. Note this tax is separate from and additive to the out-of-band findings above.
